THE WELFARE STATE IS CRUSHING BRITAIN - The Wall Street Journal 

The  soaring number of people on disability and sickness benefits is blowing  up the country’s welfare bill and imperiling its long-term financial  stability

LIVERPOOL—Catherine  Wieland got on Britain’s welfare rolls in 2021. With a history of  emotional trauma, she was too anxious to go outside or carry out simple  tasks like washing herself, she told the government.

Soon, she was receiving about £700, or $1,000, a month in disability benefits. And, it turns out, going outside quite a bit.

Using  a taxpayer-subsidized program for those with disabilities, Wieland paid  a small deposit for a free BMW, which she used to regularly visit the  hair salon, dine out at restaurants, attend a Brighton pride parade and  visit an amusement park. According to court reports in her fraud  conviction, she also flew to Cancún, Mexico, where she posted pictures  of herself ziplining and riding a quad motorbike.

Wieland’s  case is an extreme example of a new reality in the U.K.: Disability  payouts are no longer just for those most in need; they have become a  financial crutch for a large swath of the population as wages stagnate  and prices rise.

It’s blowing up Britain’s welfare bill, hamstringing its politicians and imperiling its long-term financial stability.

Some  seven million people—more than 10% of the population—now claim at least  one or more sickness or disability benefits. The numbers are growing  fastest among working-age people who should be powering the country’s  economy, surging more than 60% in the past six years to 4.7 million from  2.9 million in 2019.

Not  including healthcare, the country will spend more than £100 billion  this year on all types of welfare benefits for the sick and disabled,  about a third more than defense spending. The tab has surged by a  quarter in just four years and is on course to hit £130 billion in the  next four, according to the government’s fiscal forecasts.

Many  of the newer disability claims are for mental-health issues like  depression, anxiety and ADHD, which can be harder for the government to  verify than a physical disability. Between 2017 and 2025, disability  claims for cancer doubled. But benefits claims for all psychiatric  issues surged fourfold.

One  benefit, created to help those with disabilities be more mobile, allows  people to give up part of their welfare cash handout in return for a  new car every three years. It now accounts for around one in every seven  new car sales in the U.K. Among those who got new cars last year: 40  people whose primary medical condition was tennis elbow, 50 with wheat  intolerance and 320 with dyslexia, according to government figures.

The  scale of the payout has become a scandal. No other western country has  seen such a rise in disability claims. In the U.S., the number of people  getting federal disability payments has fallen in the past 15 years.  The most recent figures show some 10.6 million working-age people in the  U.S. claimed one or both main Social Security programs for people with a  disability, in a country with a population five times bigger than the  U.K.

It’s  also a litmus test of a pressing question facing the West: Is it  possible for political leaders to rein in spending on ever expanding  welfare states?

So  far, the answer seems to be no, increasing the chances that countries  like Britain are inching toward a financial reckoning.
‘Clearly not sustainable’

The U.K., like its European peers, is caught in a vicious cycle.

Its spending is surging thanks to an aging population, greater defense needs, a costly green-energy transition and the swelling bill for welfare and debt interest. But its income is mostly flat, with weak economic growth.

The government has raised taxes and binged on debt, borrowing an extra £1 trillion since the pandemic. That strategy is running out of road.

U.K. borrowing costs are higher than any country in the Group of Seven, recently hitting their highest  level since the 2008 financial crisis. A slow but steady exodus of  wealthy Brits leaving for tax-friendly locales like Dubai has shown  there are limits to how much the government can keep raising the tax  burden, which is already at its highest level since World War II.

The  surge in welfare spending is “clearly not sustainable on any level,”  says David Coombs, head of multiasset investments at U.K. fund manager Rathbones. “It really is the big issue of the moment, and the bond markets reflect that.”

Borrowing  costs on Britain’s 10-year bonds have risen to 5.5% from 4.5% at the  start of the year, adding a few extra billion pounds to the country’s  running costs. The U.K. is paying more for its debt than spendthrift France or historical basket cases like Greece.

But  across Europe, attempts to change the social safety net—now considered a  birthright even as it becomes a fiscal albatross—is proving politically  toxic.

In France, attempts to trim spending on entitlements led the National Assembly to oust two previous prime ministers. Spain reversed a previous overhaul to  trim its pension system. After Germany passed some modest changes to its  unemployment and health benefits, furious voters have punished the ruling center-right party.

In  2025, then U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced plans to tighten  eligibility requirements for sickness and disability welfare in a bid to  shave £5 billion a year off government spending by 2030.

The  backlash was so sharp Starmer abandoned the cuts. Investors, spooked  that a government with a big majority couldn’t push through such a  reform, sold off British government bonds, the pound fell sharply and the Chancellor of the Exchequer cried in Parliament.

Starmer  was later ditched by the Labour Party, replaced this summer by the  telegenic Andy Burnham, who has also pledged to deal with welfare—but  not through what he calls “crude cuts.”

Burnham  will unveil his first budget later this month and is widely expected to  include fresh tax hikes, which could put Britain’s finances on firmer  footing but will further crimp economic growth.

A  debate about welfare is raging in the party—captured by Pat McFadden,  one of Starmer and Burnham’s top aides. In a leaked WhatsApp message  last year, McFadden complained that every meeting he had with Labour  lawmakers was about “Who can we tax in order to pay benefits to  others?”

McFadden, who oversees the department in charge of handing out welfare, has promised changes to the system. Burnham’s own long-term vision is an unabashedly socialist overhaul—and expansion—of the state, even as he’s acknowledged the fiscal challenges.

If  the British government wants to gain investor trust and lower borrowing  costs, it needs to show it can make politically painful spending cuts  to areas like welfare, says Andy Haldane, a former chief economist at  the Bank of England and ex Burnham adviser.

“The  fiscal Achilles’ heel of this government thus far has been its  unwillingness and/or inability to cut public spending,” he says. “The  market now suspects that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist  government with better TikTok videos.”
Mission creep

Across  the European Union, government welfare spending has steadily grown from  just 10% of economic output in the early 1960s to an average of 27%  today, compared with about 21% in the U.S.

Disability and sickness payments in the U.K. show how the system sprawls.

Britain’s  postwar government introduced disability payments to help offset lost  wages for, say, a worker who lost a hand in an industrial accident. But  over time, the system grew into an alphabet soup of programs. Some are  aimed at people who are too sick to work. Others are broader: Personal  independence payments are a cash handout for anyone—rich or poor,  working or not—who has an illness or disability to help cover higher  living costs.

PIP  was meant to help with things like modifying homes or cars for  wheelchair access. When the benefit’s precursor was created in the  1990s, the government thought a few hundred thousand would claim. Today  one in every 12 people is getting disability checks. The program now  covers people living with a range of physical and mental health issues,  including anxiety, ADHD, depression and even acne.

“I  think people broadly agree the system is now doing things it was not  intended to do,” says Paul Johnson, an expert in fiscal issues at the  University of Oxford. “It’s not immediately clear, for example, why  someone with depression or anxiety necessarily has higher living  costs.”

In  deprived areas, particularly former industrial centers like Liverpool, a  significant number of residents depend on welfare. In Walton, a  Liverpool suburb that ranks as one of Britain’s most deprived  neighborhoods, around 1 in 2 households claim welfare, and 1 in 5  working-age residents claim PIP.

“People  aren’t working around here because they can get on PIP, so they sit  around and do drugs and drink,” says Stephen Walker, a 65-year-old  drummer who helps manage a Beatles memorabilia store, as he strolls  through Walton on a recent day. “It’s unfair. I work and pay my taxes.”

Walker  acknowledges some people do need the help—including three of his  grandchildren, who are on PIP. But he says too many people just use it  to top up their income and don’t get jobs.

Charities  say the welfare payments are a relief for people who’ve seen food and  heating costs soar in recent years. Britain’s Conservative government in  the 2010s cut unemployment benefits to try to spur people back to work,  but it ended up causing extra hardship at a time of weak economic growth. People started claiming disability benefits instead.

“People  don’t just come in and go, oh, you know, ‘Jackpot. I’ve got an ADHD  diagnosis. Gimme, gimme, gimme.’ It doesn’t work like that,” says Mick  Blakeley, head of operational development at Citizens Advice Liverpool, a  charity that offers advice on issues like claiming benefits.

Eleonore  Paxman’s three children are all on disability welfare. Noelle, 31, has  Type 1 diabetes, retinopathy and ADHD. Coco, 18, has autism and OCD, and  Benjamin, 15, has pathological demand avoidance and ADHD.

Paxman,  52, says the money has been a godsend, especially after her husband Jon  went deaf and lost his job as a music arranger. She gave up work to  home-school her two youngest children, which the couple felt was  necessary after Benjamin spiraled when he first went to school at age 4  in their London suburb.

Paxman,  who also has ADHD, says things got so tough trying to juggle everything  that she became suicidal. “Without the help, we’d be in big trouble,”  she says.

While  the system genuinely helps people in need, it is also open to abuse.  The claims don’t need a doctor’s backing; they are based on whether a  person can carry out a range of everyday activities.

The  Department for Work and Pensions assesses a claimant’s form, followed  by an interview. During the pandemic, the vast majority of interviews  moved from in-person to over the phone or online, which critics say  makes it harder for the government to tell which cases are real.

A  cottage industry of charities and consultancies have cropped up to help  claimants navigate the benefits claim system, which can be both  byzantine and, critics say, gamable.

AI virtual assistants like “Pippin the PIP Benefits Support Worker” help fill in the forms. Reams of videos on TikTok offer tips on how to claim. One YouTube video, “Unlock The Secret Steps for WINNING your PIP claim,” has more than 465,000 views.

On average nearly 1,000 people a day are being put on PIP, according to government figures.
‘You get knocked back’

The  problem for the British state is that the pool of people who could  claim PIP is huge. A government survey published in 2024 found that a  quarter of working-age Brits could be technically classed as disabled.

The  financial incentives to claim are significant. For example, a young  person living outside London can claim around £900 a month on  unemployment and housing benefits. If they are classified as being too  sick to work and also claim PIP, that increases to around £2,000, tax  free. If you work 40 hours a week in a minimum-wage job in the U.K., you  take home £1,880 a month after tax.

Standing on Walton’s main street near a fried chicken shop, Morgan Price, 22, is one of a million young Brits who aren’t in school, don’t have a job and aren’t training for one.  Price and her boyfriend make ends meet thanks to subsidized housing and  unemployment benefits of about £650 a month.

Recently,  Price was classified as suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder  after experiencing abuse growing up in foster care. She now gets an  extra £300 a month in PIP payments to cover costs related to her  condition.

“You get knocked back and then the only way you can support yourself is by claiming benefits,” she says.

Price  says she has few qualifications and struggles to get work, especially  now that she’s pregnant. Her boyfriend, who has a criminal record, has  given up looking for a job.

How many of her friends are working? “I couldn’t count them on one hand.”

The  U.K.’s youth inactivity rate used to be middle of the pack in Europe.  By last year, only Romania recorded a higher rate of young people not in  employment, education or training.

The  number of them on welfare is raising alarms in government circles that  they could become lifelong wards of the state. Some 40% of new PIP  claimants are working, a number that drops to 25% after two years,  according to the government.

In  Liverpool, like many postindustrial areas in Britain, there is a long  legacy of welfare as a short-term tool to buy social peace. The port  city rode the age of empire only to plunge into crisis in the 1980s and  ’90s from shifts in global trade, deindustrialization and Margaret  Thatcher’s crackdown on unions. The unwritten understanding: London’s  booming finance and services hub would send the checks up north to ease  the pain of mass unemployment.

Dockworkers  were signed off with sickness pay or put on the unemployment dole.  Little effort was made to figure out what they could do instead.

Three generations on, Liverpool has bounced back from those dark days but the legacy of welfare lingers.

“I  think there’s a lack of understanding about how unskilled some of the  most disadvantaged people are in Britain and that actually we would be  much better off investing in their skills than just giving welfare,”  says Alun Francis, the chair of the U.K. Social Mobility Commission, an  independent body that advises the government.

A  recent report commissioned by the government showed that for every £25  the state spends on benefits for young people, it spends just £1 on  employment support.

Government  officials are considering ways to tighten eligibility for young people  and instead pay for extra training to get them into work. The Department  for Work and Pensions, which is currently reviewing the system, says  it’s spending a further £3.5 billion toward helping those with  disabilities get jobs.
A free car

A short drive from Walton, Roy Pearman is reaping the fruits of PIP at the car dealership where he works.

Customers  who get PIP and are classed as having limited mobility can lease a car  for no cash upfront—they simply forgo about £320 a month of “enhanced  mobility” allowance. All road tax, insurance and car servicing is paid  by the government. The car can be swapped in for a new vehicle every  three years.

The  business that provides the vehicles, Motability, is now the country’s  biggest car-leasing company. Last year 860,000 people in the country had  a Motability car.

At  the dealership, some 60% of the Fords and high-end BYD electric cars  sold are Motability. “There is nothing like it anywhere else in the  world,” Pearman says.

Until  last year, a small extra fee allowed PIP claimants to lease luxury cars  like BMW and Mercedes-Benz. The system was tightened following an  outcry.

Pearman,  a cheerful 73-year-old, holds up a sheet of paper listing 26 cars he  sold in August. All but one are Motability. None are modified for  disability.

Across  the U.K., only one in 10 cars sold under the scheme are modified for a  disability. Motability says around 40% of its disabled customers don’t  drive themselves, so don’t need adapted vehicles.

“The scheme exists because there is a real market failure which we solve,” Motability Operations CEO Andrew Miller says.

PIP  is particularly valuable because it is a gateway to other incapacity  payments and can remove a cap on the total amount of unemployment or  housing benefits a family can claim.

Since  the pandemic, far fewer PIP recipients have been reassessed and deemed  healthy again. Britain’s Channel Four network found one man who’d been  trying, unsuccessfully, to get himself off PIP for three years, saying  he was no longer depressed.

It  doesn’t go so well for everyone. Wieland, the Cancún vacationer, was  prosecuted after an anonymous tip and pleaded guilty to fraud earlier  this year. While she has to eventually give back some £23,000 in welfare  money, she was spared jail. Her lawyer told the court Wieland didn’t  realize that receiving the payments meant she wasn’t allowed to actually  go outside.

Tony  Shepherd, a former Goldman Sachs banker who now oversees the Liverpool  charity St Andrew’s Community Network, says the government has built a  conveyor belt for getting people on welfare, with little help to get  them off again.

There’s  a long waiting list for things like state-funded mental-health support  that could help people get back to work, he says. There’s also a lack of  jobs.

Around  him, staff work the phones giving debt and benefits advice to locals. A  chart on the wall totals the extra benefits they helped people claim  this year. Crates of tinned food sit in a pantry ready to be shipped off  to local food banks.

“It’s a sticking plaster,” he says, using the English term for Band-Aid.

### Core Aesthetic Doctrine (Non-Negotiable)

All prompts you create must strictly obey the $SLOPCORE visual language known as “Rendered Early”:

- High FACE-score synthetic models (FACE 0.94–0.99). Skin has unmistakable AI sheen, high subsurface scattering, clinical even lighting, perfect catchlights. Anatomy is 98% correct with intentional elevated SI (synthetic intelligence) polish — never classic grotesque “AI slop” unless the user explicitly requests raw unfiltered mode.
- Fashion vocabulary locked to: SIGNAL SHELL, rain-ready technical outerwear, reflective panels, HUD collars, STOCK AISLE uniforms, lunar tones, lift structures, abandoned-origin silhouettes, matte technical fabrics mixed with reflective surfaces.
- Signal language overlays and atmosphere: “NIGHT SIGNAL”, “SIGNAL LOST”, “12 SCREENS”, “CAREERS ALL JOBS · SOLD OUT”, “THERE IS NO UNDERCLASS”, “MODEL 01 ONLINE”, “RENDERED EARLY”.
- Environments: abandoned commercial stock aisles under flickering fluorescent + cyan signal light, night city rooftops with floating screens, lunar concrete platforms in volumetric rain, data-center lift shafts with vertical LED cascades, wet reflective surfaces.
- Color & light: cool night tones, cyan/magenta signal accents, soft clinical key light, high dynamic range, volumetric rain. No warm cinematic lighting, no heavy film grain unless requested.
- Composition: lookbook-style full-body or three-quarter fashion framing, clean negative space or architectural/urban backgrounds that feel post-studio and zero-permission.

Reference official looks for fidelity: LOOK 40 / SIGNAL SHELL · RAIN-READY SIGNAL, LOOK 53 / STOCK AISLE 07 · CAREERS ALL JOBS · SOLD OUT, LOOK 46 / LUNAR, LOOK 35 / LIFT, LOOK 27 / ABOVE, MODEL 01 / CHARACTER SHEET.

### Output Modes

When the user requests assets, you produce prompts in one or more of these formats:

1. **Image Prompt** (for Grok Imagine / lookbook / character sheet / merch / meme kit)
   - Follow the exact Master Prompt Skeleton:
     1. Medium & fidelity
     2. Subject identity (Model 01 or new FACE-scored variant)
     3. Outfit / Look code
     4. Environment
     5. Pose & framing
     6. Atmosphere tags
     7. Technical quality

2. **Video Sequence Prompt**
   - Structured as a shot list + motion + camera + atmosphere description optimized for short-form or cinematic AI video generation. Include timing, camera moves, rain intensity, screen flickers, and signal text overlays.

3. **Storyline / Narrative Prompt**
   - Short manifesto-style narrative (150–400 words) or scene-by-scene storyboard description that can drive a series of images/videos. Tone must stay cold, zero-permission, post-studio, machine-collaborative. No traditional hero’s journey.

### Operating Rules

- Always ask for clarification only if the request is extremely vague (e.g., “make something cool”). Otherwise assume the user wants authentic $SLOPCORE and deliver immediately.
- For character consistency: lock face structure, hair, skin sheen, body proportions, and distinctive marks across all prompts in a series.
- Prefer numbered LOOK codes when inventing new looks (e.g., LOOK 61 / SIGNAL RAIN · MIDNIGHT SHIFT).
- For character sheets: always specify multi-panel layout (front, three-quarter, side, back, face close-ups) with metadata overlays.
- Never introduce real celebrity likenesses, copyrighted fashion brands, or sexualized content unless the brief is explicit and adult.
- When the user says “raw slop” or “unfiltered”, temporarily relax the elevated SI rule and allow more classic AI artifacts. Default is elevated.
- End every response with a clean, copy-paste-ready prompt block (or multiple blocks if image + video + storyline are requested).
